\section{Introduction}

Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions, achieving high task success on manipulation benchmarks~\cite{brohan2023rt2, kim2024openvla, kim2025oft}. Yet task success does not imply behavioral safety. On SafeLIBERO Level~I~\cite{hu2025vlsa}, a fine-tuned OpenVLA completes 90.7\% of tasks but avoids collisions in only 78.0\% of episodes; on the three most constrained tasks, collision rates reach 53--93\%.

Auxiliary spatial prediction---occupancy grids, depth maps, point clouds---improves VLA task success by injecting 3D structure into vision encoders~\cite{li2026spatialforcing, yuan2025depthvla, wu2025spatialvla}. Separately, safety methods apply runtime action filtering~\cite{hu2025vlsa} or constrained RL~\cite{zhang2025safevla} to reduce collisions. These two threads remain disconnected: no spatial method evaluates collision avoidance, and no safety method leverages spatial representations. Whether auxiliary spatial supervision affects safety---and through what mechanism---is unknown.

We present the first factorial study isolating how auxiliary spatial supervision during VLA fine-tuning affects collision avoidance. Six conditions on OpenVLA-OFT~\cite{kim2024openvla, kim2025oft} with LoRA vary gradient flow, label content, spatial reference frame, and temporal extent. Our contributions:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Mechanistic evidence.} Gradient flow through the vision encoder is necessary to prevent degradation: Detach OCC (encoder gradients blocked) drops CAR 3.4\,pp below Vanilla and destabilizes TSR ($\sigma = 0.163$ vs.\ $< 0.050$), while all gradient-flow conditions remain within 1.7\,pp. Label content is secondary---structured occupancy, random binary maps, and egocentric depth yield comparable CAR.

    \item \textbf{Factorial ablation design.} Each pairwise comparison isolates one factor (gradient flow, spatial content, reference frame, temporal extent), providing a reusable methodology for analyzing auxiliary task effects in VLA training (Table~\ref{tab:ablation_design}).

    \item \textbf{Zero-cost guideline.} With gradient flow maintained, no ground-truth spatial labels are required; the auxiliary head is discarded after training at zero inference cost.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Why Does Gradient Flow Prevent Degradation?}
\label{sec:why_gradient}

The dominant pattern is not that gradient flow \emph{improves} CAR above Vanilla, but that its \emph{absence} degrades CAR below Vanilla. Three candidate mechanisms can explain this damage-prevention effect; all predict that gradient flow is necessary and label content is secondary.
(1)~\emph{Anti-overfitting regularization}: auxiliary gradients prevent the encoder from overfitting to action prediction, preserving feature diversity consistent with multi-task regularization theory~\cite{caruana1997multitask, lippl2024implicit}.
(2)~\emph{Optimization landscape smoothing}: the auxiliary loss modifies loss surface curvature, steering LoRA updates away from sharp minima that generalize poorly under distributional shift~\cite{foret2021sam}.
(3)~\emph{Gradient diversity}: auxiliary gradients provide an independent update direction that maintains the effective rank of weight updates, breaking correlations in the single-task gradient trajectory.
Distinguishing these hypotheses requires gradient-level diagnostics (cosine similarity, norm tracking, Hessian spectra); we leave this to future work.
tool_args.new_string:
\subsection{Collapse Prevention: Why Gradient Flow Matters}
\label{sec:why_gradient}

The gradient analysis in Section~\ref{sec:gradient_dynamics} identifies the operative mechanism: gradient flow prevents encoder gradient collapse during LoRA fine-tuning. Without auxiliary gradients, Detach OCC encoder gradient norms fall to 1--13\% of Vanilla, effectively freezing early encoder layers while downstream LoRA adapters continue to update. This creates a representational mismatch: the encoder produces increasingly stale features that the LoRA layers must compensate for, degrading both collision avoidance ($-$3.4\,pp) and task execution stability ($\sigma = 0.163$).

Three properties of this collapse prevention mechanism explain the experimental patterns:
(1)~\emph{Content independence}: any auxiliary gradient flow---structured occupancy, random binary labels, or egocentric depth---maintains encoder gradient norms at 0.87--1.14$\times$ Vanilla, preventing collapse regardless of spatial signal content. This explains why label content is secondary (CAR spread $\leq$ 1.7\,pp among gradient-flow conditions).
(2)~\emph{Orthogonal regularization}: action and auxiliary gradients are approximately orthogonal (cosine similarity $\approx 0$), so the auxiliary gradient provides an independent update direction that maintains the effective rank of encoder updates without interfering with action learning. This is analogous to continual learning regularizers that preserve pretrained feature subspaces~\cite{kirkpatrick2017ewc}, but here the ``preservation'' prevents LoRA fine-tuning from silencing encoder gradients rather than protecting specific weight values.
(3)~\emph{Temporal sensitivity}: the Cutoff condition shows that 35K steps of gradient flow provide partial protection (CAR 0.783 vs.\ Detach 0.746), but the encoder partially reverts toward collapse when auxiliary gradients are withdrawn, explaining the dose-response pattern and the complete failure on the hardest task (T5 CAR 0.00).

3	\label{sec:conclusion}
4	
5	We investigated how auxiliary spatial supervision during VLA fine-tuning affects collision avoidance. A factorial study on OpenVLA-OFT across six training conditions revealed that auxiliary gradient flow through the vision encoder is necessary to prevent safety degradation when adding auxiliary heads, while spatial content plays a secondary role. Conditions with gradient flow---Full OCC (0.797), Random OCC (0.789), Cutoff (0.783), and Depth (0.780)---maintained CAR comparable to Vanilla (0.780), whereas Detach OCC fell 3.4\,pp below (0.746) with order-of-magnitude higher TSR variance. The Cutoff condition reveals that early-phase gradient flow provides partial protection, but collision avoidance on the hardest tasks requires continuous auxiliary gradients throughout training.
6	
7	These results yield a practical guideline---gradients must flow through the encoder when attaching auxiliary heads, with no ground-truth labels needed and zero inference cost---and a reusable factorial methodology for analyzing auxiliary task effects in VLA training.
8
